<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1280 720">
    <!-- 模板: 封面页 - 麦肯锡风格 (精装版) -->
    
    <defs>
        <!-- 顶部渐变条 -->
        <linearGradient id="headerGrad" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
            <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:#005587"/>
            <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:#0076A8"/>
        </linearGradient>
        <!-- 装饰渐变 -->
        <linearGradient id="decoGrad" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="100%">
            <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:#005587;stop-opacity:0.12"/>
            <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:#0076A8;stop-opacity:0.04"/>
        </linearGradient>
    </defs>
    
    <!-- 白色背景 -->
    <rect width="1280" height="720" fill="#FFFFFF"/>

    <!-- 左侧主装饰条 -->
    <rect x="0" y="0" width="12" height="720" fill="url(#headerGrad)"/>
    
    <!-- 左侧副装饰条 -->
    <rect x="12" y="0" width="3" height="720" fill="#F5A623"/>

    <!-- 左上角装饰组合 -->
    <rect x="60" y="55" width="180" height="5" fill="#005587"/>
    <rect x="60" y="65" width="100" height="3" fill="#0076A8" fill-opacity="0.5"/>
    
    <!-- 右侧大面积装饰区 -->
    <rect x="780" y="0" width="500" height="720" fill="url(#decoGrad)"/>
    
    <!-- 几何装饰元素 -->
    <rect x="850" y="120" width="360" height="360" fill="none" stroke="#005587" stroke-width="1" stroke-opacity="0.15"/>
    <rect x="900" y="170" width="260" height="260" fill="none" stroke="#005587" stroke-width="1" stroke-opacity="0.1"/>
    <rect x="950" y="220" width="160" height="160" fill="#005587" fill-opacity="0.03"/>
    
    <!-- 三角装饰 -->
    <path d="M 1050,140 L 1220,140 L 1135,320 Z" fill="#005587" fill-opacity="0.06"/>
    <path d="M 880,400 L 1000,400 L 940,520 Z" fill="#0076A8" fill-opacity="0.05"/>

    <!-- 主标题区域 -->
    <text x="60" y="260" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="56" font-weight="bold" fill="#2C3E50" letter-spacing="-1">
        {{TITLE}}
    </text>
    <text x="60" y="330" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="56" font-weight="bold" fill="#2C3E50" letter-spacing="-1">
        {{TITLE_LINE2}}
    </text>

    <!-- 副标题 -->
    <text x="60" y="400" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#5D6D7E" letter-spacing="0.5">
        {{SUBTITLE}}
    </text>

    <!-- 分隔线组合 -->
    <line x1="60" y1="450" x2="500" y2="450" stroke="#ECF0F1" stroke-width="2"/>
    <line x1="60" y1="456" x2="200" y2="456" stroke="#005587" stroke-width="2"/>

    <!-- 项目信息区 -->
    <rect x="60" y="520" width="400" height="100" fill="#F8F9FA" rx="4"/>
    <rect x="60" y="520" width="4" height="100" fill="#005587" rx="2"/>
    
    <text x="84" y="555" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#7F8C8D">PROJECT CODE</text>
    <text x="84" y="580" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#2C3E50">{{PROJECT_CODE}}</text>
    
    <line x1="260" y1="535" x2="260" y2="605" stroke="#ECF0F1" stroke-width="1"/>
    
    <text x="284" y="555" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#7F8C8D">DATE</text>
    <text x="284" y="580" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#2C3E50">{{DATE}}</text>

    <!-- 底部装饰线 -->
    <line x1="60" y1="680" x2="1220" y2="680" stroke="#ECF0F1" stroke-width="1"/>
    
    <!-- 机密标识 -->
    <rect x="1080" y="655" width="140" height="28" fill="#005587" fill-opacity="0.08" rx="4"/>
    <text x="1150" y="675" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#005587" letter-spacing="1">
        CONFIDENTIAL
    </text>

    <!-- 页码 -->
    <text x="60" y="700" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#7F8C8D">{{PAGE_NUM}}</text>

</svg>

  <text x="85" y="116" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#27AE60">HISTORIC ACHIEVEMENT</text>
  <text x="265" y="116" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#5D6D7E">Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 — the only human disease ever eliminated through a global vaccination campaign</text>

  <!-- ===== TIMELINE SECTION ===== -->
  <!-- Timeline backbone -->
  <line x1="100" y1="280" x2="1180" y2="280" stroke="url(#timelineGrad)" stroke-width="4"/>

  <!-- Timeline title -->
  <text x="640" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#2C3E50">The Road to Eradication: 1796–1980</text>

  <!-- Milestone 1: 1796 -->
  <circle cx="100" cy="280" r="14" fill="#005587"/>
  <text x="100" y="285" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">1796</text>
  <rect x="30" y="180" width="140" height="80" fill="#EEF4FA" stroke="#005587" stroke-width="1.5" rx="5"/>
  <line x1="100" y1="260" x2="100" y2="266" stroke="#005587" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="100" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#005587">1796</text>
  <text x="100" y="218" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">Edward Jenner</text>
  <text x="100" y="234" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">creates first</text>
  <text x="100" y="250" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">vaccine</text>

  <!-- Milestone 2: 1959 -->
  <circle cx="370" cy="280" r="14" fill="#0076A8"/>
  <text x="370" y="285" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">1959</text>
  <rect x="300" y="180" width="140" height="80" fill="#EEF4FA" stroke="#0076A8" stroke-width="1.5" rx="5"/>
  <line x1="370" y1="260" x2="370" y2="266" stroke="#0076A8" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="370" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#0076A8">1959</text>
  <text x="370" y="218" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">WHO resolution</text>
  <text x="370" y="234" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">to eradicate</text>
  <text x="370" y="250" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">smallpox globally</text>

  <!-- Milestone 3: 1967 -->
  <circle cx="640" cy="280" r="14" fill="#00796B"/>
  <text x="640" y="285" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">1967</text>
  <rect x="570" y="180" width="140" height="80" fill="#E8F5F3" stroke="#00796B" stroke-width="1.5" rx="5"/>
  <line x1="640" y1="260" x2="640" y2="266" stroke="#00796B" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="640" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#00796B">1967</text>
  <text x="640" y="218" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">WHO intensified</text>
  <text x="640" y="234" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">eradication</text>
  <text x="640" y="250" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">campaign launched</text>

  <!-- Milestone 4: 1977 -->
  <circle cx="910" cy="280" r="14" fill="#F5A623"/>
  <text x="910" y="285" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">1977</text>
  <rect x="840" y="180" width="140" height="80" fill="#FFF8E1" stroke="#F5A623" stroke-width="1.5" rx="5"/>
  <line x1="910" y1="260" x2="910" y2="266" stroke="#F5A623" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="910" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#E89207">1977</text>
  <text x="910" y="218" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">Last natural case</text>
  <text x="910" y="234" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">of smallpox</text>
  <text x="910" y="250" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">Somalia</text>

  <text x="1180" y="285" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">1980</text>
  <rect x="1100" y="155" width="160" height="110" fill="#E8F8EF" stroke="#27AE60" stroke-width="2" rx="5"/>
  <line x1="1180" y1="258" x2="1180" y2="265" stroke="#27AE60" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="1180" y="176" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#27AE60">1980</text>

  <text x="1180" y="213" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2C3E50">GLOBAL</text>
  <text x="1180" y="231" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#27AE60">ERADICATION</text>

  <text x="1180" y="263" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#5D6D7E">Jenner's vaccine</text>

  <!-- ===== WHY SMALLPOX WAS ERADICABLE — 3 CARDS ===== -->
  <text x="640" y="335" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#2C3E50">Why Smallpox Was Uniquely Suited for Eradication</text>

  <!-- Card 1: Human-only host -->
  <rect x="60" y="352" width="360" height="260" fill="#F4F7F6" stroke="#D5E0DC" stroke-width="1.5" rx="8"/>

  <use data-icon="globe" x="220" y="375" width="44" height="44" fill="#005587"/>
  <text x="240" y="440" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#005587">Human-Only Host</text>
  <text x="240" y="466" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">The virus infected only humans —</text>
  <text x="240" y="484" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">no animal reservoir to maintain</text>
  <text x="240" y="502" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">transmission between outbreaks</text>
  <text x="240" y="528" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#7F8C8D">This made eradication theoretically</text>
  <text x="240" y="546" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#7F8C8D">possible — eliminate human-to-human</text>
  <text x="240" y="564" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#7F8C8D">spread and the disease disappears</text>
  <text x="240" y="590" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#95A5A6" font-style="italic">No animal reservoir</text>

  <!-- Card 2: Visible symptoms -->
  <rect x="460" y="352" width="360" height="260" fill="#F4F7F6" stroke="#D5E0DC" stroke-width="1.5" rx="8"/>
  <rect x="460" y="352" width="360" height="6" fill="#00796B" rx="3"/>
  <use data-icon="eye" x="620" y="375" width="44" height="44" fill="#00796B"/>
  <text x="640" y="440" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#00796B">Distinguishable Symptoms</text>
  <text x="640" y="466" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">The distinctive pustular rash</text>
  <text x="640" y="484" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">made smallpox easily identifiable</text>
  <text x="640" y="502" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">by health workers in the field</text>
  <text x="640" y="528" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#7F8C8D">Enabled targeted ring vaccination:</text>
  <text x="640" y="546" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#7F8C8D">vaccinate contacts of confirmed</text>
  <text x="640" y="564" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#7F8C8D">cases to contain spread rapidly</text>
  <text x="640" y="590" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#95A5A6" font-style="italic">Ring vaccination strategy</text>

  <!-- Card 3: Cheap effective vaccine -->
  <rect x="860" y="352" width="360" height="260" fill="#F4F7F6" stroke="#D5E0DC" stroke-width="1.5" rx="8"/>
  <rect x="860" y="352" width="360" height="6" fill="#27AE60" rx="3"/>
  <use data-icon="shield-check" x="1020" y="375" width="44" height="44" fill="#27AE60"/>
  <text x="1040" y="440" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#27AE60">Cheap, Effective Vaccine</text>
  <text x="1040" y="466" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">The smallpox vaccine was</text>
  <text x="1040" y="484" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">inexpensive to produce and</text>
  <text x="1040" y="502" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">highly effective at preventing disease</text>
  <text x="1040" y="528" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#7F8C8D">Accessible to low-income countries;</text>
  <text x="1040" y="546" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#7F8C8D">thermostable enough for global</text>
  <text x="1040" y="564" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#7F8C8D">deployment in tropical climates</text>
  <text x="1040" y="590" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#95A5A6" font-style="italic">Globally deployable</text>

  <!-- Footer -->
  <rect x="0" y="648" width="1280" height="72" fill="#FAFBFC"/>
  <line x1="0" y1="648" x2="1280" y2="648" stroke="#E5E7EB" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="60" y="678" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#95A5A6">Source: WHO Global Commission for the Certification of Smallpox Eradication (1980) | Our World in Data — ourworldindata.org/smallpox</text>
  <rect x="1180" y="655" width="60" height="28" fill="#00796B" rx="4"/>
  <text x="1210" y="674" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">5</text>

</svg>

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1280 720">

      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#005587"/>

  <rect width="1280" height="720" fill="#FFFFFF"/>

  <!-- Top gradient bar -->
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="5" fill="url(#headerGrad)"/>

  <!-- Header area -->

  <!-- Section badge -->
  <rect x="60" y="20" width="50" height="40" fill="#00796B" rx="4"/>
  <text x="85" y="48" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">08</text>

  <!-- Page title -->
  <text x="130" y="52" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" font-weight="bold" fill="#2C3E50">Key Takeaways: Vaccines Have Eliminated Deadly Diseases — But the Job Isn't Done</text>

  <!-- Section name -->
  <text x="1220" y="52" text-anchor="end" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#7F8C8D">Conclusions & Call to Action</text>

  <!-- ===== 2x2 GRID OF KEY FINDINGS ===== -->
  <!-- Each card: 560x210, gap 20 -->
  <!-- Row 1: y=95 to 305, Row 2: y=315 to 525 -->

  <!-- Card 1 (top-left): 100% Elimination -->
  <rect x="60" y="95" width="560" height="215" fill="#E8F8EF" stroke="#27AE60" stroke-width="2" rx="8"/>
  <rect x="60" y="95" width="560" height="6" fill="#27AE60" rx="3"/>
  <use data-icon="circle-checkmark" x="85" y="114" width="36" height="36" fill="#27AE60"/>
  <text x="140" y="136" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#27AE60">100% Elimination Achieved</text>
  <text x="85" y="170" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#2C3E50">Diphtheria, smallpox, and acute polio</text>
  <text x="85" y="190" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#2C3E50">are completely eliminated in the US</text>
  <text x="85" y="220" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">Measles cases reduced by 99.99% (3,044 → 0.2 /M/yr)</text>
  <text x="85" y="240" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">Rubella cases reduced by 99.98% (242 → 0.04 /M/yr)</text>
  <text x="85" y="260" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#7F8C8D">Smallpox: only human disease eradicated worldwide (1980)</text>
  <text x="85" y="286" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#27AE60">→ Definitive proof that vaccines can eliminate ancient killers</text>

  <!-- Card 2 (top-right): Timeline Collapse -->
  <rect x="660" y="95" width="560" height="215" fill="#EEF4FA" stroke="#005587" stroke-width="2" rx="8"/>
  <rect x="660" y="95" width="560" height="6" fill="#005587" rx="3"/>
  <use data-icon="arrow-trend-up" x="685" y="114" width="36" height="36" fill="#005587"/>
  <text x="740" y="136" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#005587">Vaccine Development Accelerating</text>
  <text x="685" y="170" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#2C3E50">From 105 years (typhoid) to under 1 year</text>
  <text x="685" y="190" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#2C3E50">(COVID-19) — a 100x compression</text>
  <!-- Small timeline bar -->
  <rect x="685" y="210" width="480" height="16" fill="#ECF0F1" rx="3"/>
  <rect x="685" y="210" width="480" height="16" fill="#005587" rx="3"/>
  <rect x="685" y="210" width="20" height="16" fill="#F5A623" rx="3"/>
  <text x="685" y="244" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#005587">1884</text>
  <text x="1120" y="244" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#005587">2020</text>
  <text x="697" y="244" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#F5A623">COVID <1yr</text>
  <text x="685" y="268" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">Enabled by mRNA technology, genome sequencing,</text>
  <text x="685" y="286" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">advanced microscopy, and virus-like particles</text>

  <!-- Card 3 (bottom-left): Herd Immunity -->
  <rect x="60" y="322" width="560" height="215" fill="#E8F5F3" stroke="#00796B" stroke-width="2" rx="8"/>
  <rect x="60" y="322" width="560" height="6" fill="#00796B" rx="3"/>
  <use data-icon="shield-check" x="85" y="341" width="36" height="36" fill="#00796B"/>
  <text x="140" y="363" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#00796B">Herd Immunity Protects Communities</text>
  <text x="85" y="397" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#2C3E50">Population-level vaccination shields newborns,</text>
  <text x="85" y="417" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#2C3E50">immunocompromised, and cancer patients</text>
  <text x="85" y="447" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">When enough people are vaccinated, pathogens</text>
  <text x="85" y="465" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">cannot spread — protecting those who cannot</text>
  <text x="85" y="483" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">receive vaccines themselves</text>
  <text x="85" y="511" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#00796B">→ Vaccination is a community obligation, not just individual choice</text>

  <!-- Card 4 (bottom-right): Gaps Remain -->
  <rect x="660" y="322" width="560" height="215" fill="#FFF5F5" stroke="#E74C3C" stroke-width="2" rx="8"/>
  <rect x="660" y="322" width="560" height="6" fill="#E74C3C" rx="3"/>
  <use data-icon="triangle-exclamation" x="685" y="341" width="36" height="36" fill="#E74C3C"/>
  <text x="740" y="363" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#E74C3C">Coverage Gaps Persist</text>
  <text x="685" y="397" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#2C3E50">Pneumococcal: only 40.5% case reduction</text>
  <text x="685" y="417" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#2C3E50">Hepatitis A: 89% | Hepatitis B: 83.9%</text>
  <text x="685" y="447" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">Access gaps, supply shortages, and trust barriers</text>
  <text x="685" y="465" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">prevent full disease control globally</text>
  <text x="685" y="483" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">Newer, more effective vaccines and improved</text>
  <text x="685" y="501" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#5D6D7E">delivery systems are urgently needed</text>
  <text x="685" y="511" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#E74C3C">→ Urgent: improve access, coverage, and trust</text>

  <!-- ===== CALL TO ACTION BANNER ===== -->
  <rect x="60" y="550" width="1160" height="74" fill="url(#ctaGrad)" rx="8"/>
  <use data-icon="lightbulb" x="90" y="566" width="36" height="36" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
  <text x="148" y="580" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">CALL TO ACTION FOR GLOBAL HEALTH SYSTEMS:</text>
  <text x="148" y="606" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#FFFFFF">Strengthen access, expand coverage, and rebuild trust — the tools exist; the imperative is political and operational.</text>

  <!-- Footer -->
  <rect x="0" y="648" width="1280" height="72" fill="#FAFBFC"/>
  <line x1="0" y1="648" x2="1280" y2="648" stroke="#E5E7EB" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="60" y="678" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#95A5A6">Source: Our World in Data — ourworldindata.org/vaccination | Roush SW and Murphy TV (2007), JAMA</text>
  <rect x="1180" y="655" width="60" height="28" fill="#00796B" rx="4"/>
  <text x="1210" y="674" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">8</text>

</svg>

arguments.content:
# 01_cover

[Transition] Welcome. Today we examine one of public health's most powerful tools — and the data behind its transformative impact.

Vaccines have reshaped human history. In the span of two centuries, we went from Edward Jenner's cowpox-based experiment to eliminating entire diseases from the face of the earth. [Pause] This presentation draws on data from Our World in Data and Roush & Murphy's landmark 2007 analysis to tell that story — in numbers.

Our goal today is threefold: understand how fast vaccine development has accelerated, quantify the dramatic reductions in disease burden, and identify where the work remains unfinished.

Key points: (1) Vaccines span 230+ years of innovation (2) Data-driven evidence on elimination and reduction (3) Remaining gaps demand action
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_vaccine_timeline

[Transition] Let's begin at the beginning — how long does it actually take to develop a vaccine?

The data tells a remarkable story of acceleration. Typhoid fever's vaccine took 105 years to develop after the pathogen was identified. [Data] One hundred and five years — that's more than a human lifetime. Yet COVID-19's vaccine was licensed in less than one year — an achievement made possible by mRNA technology and genomic tools. [Pause]

The trend is unmistakable: development timelines have collapsed. The tools of modern science — genome sequencing, virus-like particles, advanced microscopy — have transformed what once took generations into what can now happen in months.

Key points: (1) Typhoid: 105 yrs → COVID-19: <1 yr — a 100x compression (2) mRNA technology is the breakthrough enabler (3) Meningitis, polio, pertussis all took decades before modern tools
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 03_us_disease_elimination

[Transition] Now let's look at the results — what do these vaccines actually accomplish in practice?

The US data from Roush and Murphy provides a stunning answer. [Data] Four diseases — diphtheria, smallpox, acute polio, and rubella deaths — were reduced by 100%. Complete elimination. These were diseases that killed tens of thousands annually just generations ago. [Pause]

Measles fell by 99.99% — from 3,044 cases per million per year to just 0.2. That near-total elimination is visible in the table before you. But look at the bottom rows. Pneumococcal disease achieved only a 40.5% case reduction. Hepatitis A and B remain incompletely controlled. The job is not finished.

Key points: (1) 100% elimination for diphtheria, smallpox, acute polio (2) Measles: 99.99% reduction (3) Pneumococcal disease: only 40.5% — the persistent gap
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 04_measles_heatmap

[Transition] Let's zoom in on measles as a case study in what public health policy can accomplish at scale.

Before 1963, nearly every state in the US reported between 100 and 1,000+ cases per 100,000 people. [Data] That's the deep red band you see across all 50 states. Then, three pivotal interventions changed everything.

1963: John Enders develops the first measles vaccine. Incidence begins to decline, but inconsistently. 1971: The MMR vaccine combines measles, mumps, and rubella into one shot, improving uptake. 1980: Vaccination becomes mandatory for kindergarten entry. [Pause] The heatmap goes nearly white — near-zero incidence across all 50 states. Only sporadic outbreaks persist.

Key points: (1) Pre-1963: 3,044 cases/million/yr — high incidence in all states (2) 1980 mandate was the decisive turning point (3) Sporadic outbreaks remain where coverage lapses
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 05_smallpox_eradication

[Transition] If measles shows what's possible at the national level, smallpox shows what's possible globally.

Smallpox is the only human disease ever eradicated from the planet. [Pause] Think about what that means: a pathogen that killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone — gone. Certified extinct in 1980 by the WHO, 184 years after Jenner's first vaccine.

Three factors made eradication possible. First, smallpox infects only humans — no animal reservoir to hide in. Second, its pustular rash was instantly recognizable, enabling targeted ring vaccination. Third, the vaccine was cheap, effective, and thermostable enough to deploy in the tropics. Without all three, eradication would have been impossible.

[Data] WHO launched its intensified campaign in 1967. Ten years later, in 1977, the last natural case occurred in Somalia. Three years after that, in 1980, the world was declared free.

Key points: (1) Only human disease ever eradicated — certified 1980 (2) Three conditions: human-only host, visible symptoms, cheap effective vaccine (3) Model for future eradication campaigns
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 06_herd_immunity

[Transition] So far we've focused on how vaccines protect individuals. But there's a second, equally powerful mechanism: herd immunity.

Here's the critical insight: vaccination is not just a personal health decision — it is a community obligation. [Pause] When enough people are vaccinated, pathogens simply cannot find enough susceptible hosts to sustain transmission. The chain breaks.

This matters enormously for three groups who cannot protect themselves directly: newborns too young to vaccinate, immunocompromised individuals whose immune systems cannot respond effectively, and cancer patients on chemotherapy for whom vaccines may be medically contraindicated. [Data] These are the people who depend entirely on the vaccination choices of those around them.

Scenario A in the diagram shows what happens with low coverage — the pathogen hops freely through the community, reaching the vulnerable. Scenario B shows high coverage — the transmission chain breaks before it can reach anyone who cannot be protected.

Key points: (1) Herd immunity breaks transmission chains protecting the unvaccinatable (2) Three key vulnerable groups: newborns, immunocompromised, chemo patients (3) Vaccination is a social contract, not just an individual act
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 07_remaining_challenges

[Transition] With that understanding of what vaccines can achieve, we must be honest about where they have not yet succeeded.

The data reveals a clear hierarchy of control. At one end: 100% elimination. At the other: pneumococcal disease, where we've achieved only a 40.5% reduction in cases and 31.3% in deaths. [Pause] That is not a failure of the vaccine concept — it is a failure of implementation.

Hepatitis A and B show 89% and 83.9% case reductions respectively — impressive, but not complete. Why do these gaps persist? Three systemic barriers: access inequities that mean not everyone globally can receive vaccines; supply shortages that interrupt immunization windows in a child's critical first years; and trust and misinformation challenges that reduce uptake even when vaccines are available.

[Data] Pneumococcal disease: 233 pre-vaccine cases per million per year, 139 post-vaccine. That 94-case-per-million gap represents millions of preventable illnesses and tens of thousands of deaths annually.

Key points: (1) Pneumococcal: 40.5% — lowest reduction among all vaccine-preventable diseases (2) Three barriers: access, supply, trust (3) New vaccines and better delivery systems are urgently needed
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 08_takeaways

[Transition] Let me close with the four things I want you to carry out of this room.

First: vaccines work — and work definitively. We have 100% elimination of diphtheria, smallpox, and acute polio in the United States. These are not small reductions. They are complete eradication of diseases that devastated human populations for centuries. [Pause]

Second: the pace of innovation is itself a resource. Going from 105 years to under one year is not an accident — it reflects deliberate investment in mRNA platforms, genomic sequencing, and global research collaboration. That infrastructure must be sustained and expanded.

Third: herd immunity means vaccination is never only about you. It is about the newborn in the household next door. The neighbor undergoing chemotherapy. The immunocompromised colleague who cannot mount an immune response.

Fourth: gaps persist, and they have names. Pneumococcal disease at 40.5%. Hepatitis at under 90%. These gaps are not inevitable — they are addressable through political will, equitable access, and sustained engagement with communities who have lost trust in health institutions.

The tools exist. The science is settled. [Pause] The imperative now is operational and political: strengthen access, expand coverage, rebuild trust.

Key points: (1) 100% elimination proven possible (2) mRNA era: development timelines collapsed (3) Herd immunity is a social contract (4) Remaining gaps are solvable — if we choose to solve them
Duration: 3 minutes

[Transition] If measles shows what's possible at the national level, smallpox shows what's possible globally.

Smallpox is the only human disease ever eradicated from the planet. [Pause] Think about what that means: a pathogen that killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone — gone. Certified extinct in 1980 by the WHO, 184 years after Jenner's first vaccine.

Three factors made eradication possible. First, smallpox infects only humans — no animal reservoir to hide in. Second, its pustular rash was instantly recognizable, enabling targeted ring vaccination. Third, the vaccine was cheap, effective, and thermostable enough to deploy in the tropics. Without all three, eradication would have been impossible.

[Data] WHO launched its intensified campaign in 1967. Ten years later, in 1977, the last natural case occurred in Somalia. Three years after that, in 1980, the world was declared free.

Key points: (1) Only human disease ever eradicated — certified 1980 (2) Three conditions: human-only host, visible symptoms, cheap effective vaccine (3) Model for future eradication campaigns
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 06_herd_immunity

[Transition] So far we've focused on how vaccines protect individuals. But there's a second, equally powerful mechanism: herd immunity.

Here's the critical insight: vaccination is not just a personal health decision — it is a community obligation. [Pause] When enough people are vaccinated, pathogens simply cannot find enough susceptible hosts to sustain transmission. The chain breaks.

This matters enormously for three groups who cannot protect themselves directly: newborns too young to vaccinate, immunocompromised individuals whose immune systems cannot respond effectively, and cancer patients on chemotherapy for whom vaccines may be medically contraindicated. [Data] These are the people who depend entirely on the vaccination choices of those around them.

Scenario A in the diagram shows what happens with low coverage — the pathogen hops freely through the community, reaching the vulnerable. Scenario B shows high coverage — the transmission chain breaks before it can reach anyone who cannot be protected.

Key points: (1) Herd immunity breaks transmission chains protecting the unvaccinatable (2) Three key vulnerable groups: newborns, immunocompromised, chemo patients (3) Vaccination is a social contract, not just an individual act
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 07_remaining_challenges

[Transition] With that understanding of what vaccines can achieve, we must be honest about where they have not yet succeeded.

The data reveals a clear hierarchy of control. At one end: 100% elimination. At the other: pneumococcal disease, where we've achieved only a 40.5% reduction in cases and 31.3% in deaths. [Pause] That is not a failure of the vaccine concept — it is a failure of implementation.

Hepatitis A and B show 89% and 83.9% case reductions respectively — impressive, but not complete. Why do these gaps persist? Three systemic barriers: access inequities that mean not everyone globally can receive vaccines; supply shortages that interrupt immunization windows in a child's critical first years; and trust and misinformation challenges that reduce uptake even when vaccines are available.

[Data] Pneumococcal disease: 233 pre-vaccine cases per million per year, 139 post-vaccine. That 94-case-per-million gap represents millions of preventable illnesses and tens of thousands of deaths annually.

Key points: (1) Pneumococcal: 40.5% — lowest reduction among all vaccine-preventable diseases (2) Three barriers: access, supply, trust (3) New vaccines and better delivery systems are urgently needed
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 08_takeaways

[Transition] Let me close with the four things I want you to carry out of this room.

First: vaccines work — and work definitively. We have 100% elimination of diphtheria, smallpox, and acute polio in the United States. These are not small reductions. They are complete eradication of diseases that devastated human populations for centuries. [Pause]

Second: the pace of innovation is itself a resource. Going from 105 years to under one year is not an accident — it reflects deliberate investment in mRNA platforms, genomic sequencing, and global research collaboration. That infrastructure must be sustained and expanded.

Third: herd immunity means vaccination is never only about you. It is about the newborn in the household next door. The neighbor undergoing chemotherapy. The immunocompromised colleague who cannot mount an immune response.

Fourth: gaps persist, and they have names. Pneumococcal disease at 40.5%. Hepatitis at under 90%. These gaps are not inevitable — they are addressable through political will, equitable access, and sustained engagement with communities who have lost trust in health institutions.

The tools exist. The science is settled. [Pause] The imperative now is operational and political: strengthen access, expand coverage, rebuild trust.

Key points: (1) 100% elimination proven possible (2) mRNA era: development timelines collapsed (3) Herd immunity is a social contract (4) Remaining gaps are solvable — if we choose to solve them
Duration: 3 minutes

steps.message:
The presentation has been successfully exported to `/app/output/final_deck.pptx` (88KB, 8 slides).

**Pipeline complete:**
- **8 slides** generated with McKinsey-style design (healthcare teal + McKinsey blue palette)
- **Slide 02**: Horizontal bar chart showing 9 diseases from 105 years (typhoid) to <1 year (COVID-19), with COVID highlighted in amber
- **Slide 03**: Full data table with color-coded rows (green=100% eliminated, amber=partial, red=major gap) + 4 KPI cards
- **Slide 04**: Simulated heatmap grid with 1963/1971/1980 milestone annotations
- **Slide 05**: Timeline from 1796→1980 + three eradication-enabler cards
- **Slide 06**: Two-scenario herd immunity diagram with vulnerable group cards
- **Slide 07**: Progress bar cards for pneumococcal (40.5%), Hepatitis A (89%), Hepatitis B (83.9%) + systemic barrier cards
- **Slide 08**: 2×2 takeaway grid + teal call-to-action banner
- All data sourced exclusively from `source_brief.md`; speaker notes embedded throughout
